# 1998 S10 Blazer Getting No Brake Pedal After Repair

When a brake pedal goes to the floor immediately after a rebuild, the system has lost its ability to generate hydraulic pressure. In a properly functioning hydraulic circuit, the master cylinder acts as the pump, creating pressure that pushes fluid through lines and into calipers or wheel cylinders. If you replaced the front and rear brakes, installed new calipers, added high-pressure hoses, and bled the master cylinder itself with zero result, the issue is almost certainly not a lack of effort in bleeding. It is an air lock, a collapsed hose, or a catastrophic seal failure within the newly installed components.

The specific symptom you describedâfluid appearing at the rear driver-side caliper initially, then draining out completely when disconnectedâpoints to a compromised component rather than simple air entrapment. When you pulled that hose and fluid drained rapidly from the caliper, you confirmed that the master cylinder is pushing pressure into that line, but something downstream or within the assembly cannot contain it. This behavior suggests either an internal leak in the rear caliper piston seals or, more likely given the sudden cessation of flow, a failure of the high-pressure hose itself.

High-pressure brake hoses are critical components designed to expand slightly under load to accommodate suspension movement while maintaining pressure integrity. If a new hose is defective or was not seated correctly during installation, it can collapse under vacuum or fail internally, acting as a check valve that only allows fluid one way or simply restricting flow until the line bursts. The fact that fluid appeared initially and then stopped indicates the line may have been partially blocked by debris from old rubber degradation or a manufacturing defect in the new hose.

Before moving to more invasive diagnostics like bench testing the entire master cylinder, you must isolate the hydraulic circuit. Disconnect the front brake lines at the master cylinder and bleed only the rear system using a hand pump or pressure bleeder. If the pedal still sinks without resistance and fluid continues to leak from the rear caliper when disconnected, the rear caliper piston seals are likely blown internally. New calipers can fail immediately if the piston was not retracted properly during installation or if corrosion prevented the return spring from seating correctly, causing the piston to migrate forward and block internal passages.

If the rear system is isolated and still fails to build pressure, replace the high-pressure hose on that side with a known good unit. Do not rely on visual inspection alone; rubber hoses can fail internally while looking pristine externally. Once that line is verified as sound, reconnect the front lines and attempt to bleed the entire system again using a vacuum bleeder if possible. Vacuum bleeding removes air more effectively than gravity bleeding because it actively pulls fluid through the master cylinder reservoir, preventing air from being dragged in by the piston's movement.

If you have already replaced the master cylinder and it still yields no pressure, suspect contamination in the brake fluid or a cracked reservoir. Brake fluid is hygroscopic; if old, contaminated fluid was introduced during the repair, it can cause internal swelling of seals or corrosion within the metal body of the master cylinder, leading to immediate failure. Always flush the entire hydraulic system with fresh DOT 3 or DOT 4 fluid before reassembly to ensure no particulate matter remains from the disassembly process.

Finally, consider the proportioning valve located between the front and rear lines. If this component is clogged or has a failing internal seal, it can block fluid flow to one end of the vehicle. Disconnect the line at the master cylinder side of the proportioning valve and try to bleed directly into that port. If pressure builds there but not in the calipers, the valve is the culprit. Addressing these specific failure points systematically will restore the hydraulic integrity required for safe braking on your 1998 S10 Blazer.
